title: Part Four: Valuation Process

PART FOUR (4)

VALUATION PROCESS

 

BASIS OF VALUATION

{{valuation.basis_statement}}

 

DEFINITION OF MARKET VALUE

For the purpose of this valuation "Market Value" as defined by the RICS Valuation – Global Standards (the Red Book, effective 31 January 2022) is the estimated amount for which an asset should exchange on the date of valuation between a willing seller and a buyer in an arms' length transaction after proper marketing, wherein the parties had each acted knowledgeably, prudently and without compulsion.

By the above definition:

  1. "The estimated amount" means; most probable price expressed in terms of money to be reasonably obtained in the market at the date of valuation.
  2. "a property should exchange" means; the fact that the value of a property is an estimated amount, rather than actual sale price.
  3. "on the date of valuation" means; the estimated Market Value is time specific as of a given date. This is because markets and market conditions may change; the estimated value may be incorrect or inappropriate at another time.
  4. "between a willing buyer" means; one who purchases in accordance with the realities of the current market. The assumed buyer would not pay a higher price than the market requires.
  5. "a willing seller" means; a hypothetical owner who is motivated to sell the property at the best price attainable.
  6. "in an arm's length transaction" means; a transaction which is between parties who do not have a particular or special relationship. It is therefore presumed to be between unrelated parties each acting independently.
  7. "after proper marketing" means; The property would be exposed to the market in the most appropriate manner. The length of exposure time may vary with market conditions, but must be sufficient to allow adequate participation of potential purchasers.
  8. "wherein the parties had each acted knowledgeably" presumes; the willing buyer and the willing seller are reasonably well informed about the nature and characteristics of the property.
  9. "and without compulsion" means; that each party is motivated to undertake the transaction, but neither is forced or unduly coerced to complete it.

 

VALUATION METHODOLOGY

In determining the Market Value of the subject property, the {{valuation.methods_applied}} {{valuation.methods_used_verb}} considered and applied. The choice of method(s) is dependent on the type and nature of the property, the availability of relevant data, and the purpose of valuation. The applied method(s) of valuation are briefly described below:

{{#if methods.has_comparable_sales}}

 

1. The Direct Comparison or Market Comparison Method

This method of valuation involves the systematic comparison of value-determining features among similar properties such as lot size, location, financing terms, market conditions at the time of sale, etc and usually the features of the subject property which is being evaluated are compared with several neighbouring or similar properties that have been sold recently (known as Comparable properties).

The sale price of each Comparable is adjusted to reflect the ways in which the subject property is more or less different from the Comparable. There would not have been adjustments if the Comparable properties were exactly like the subject property and the transactional details were the same. However, the real estate market is imperfect and no two properties are exactly alike and therefore some forms of adjustment is almost always required.

After the adjustment, the valuer reconciles the final adjusted prices into an indicated value.

In adopting the sale comparison approach a careful value analysis was made on recently completed sale transactions of similar properties as well as the quoted prices of {{property.property_type_lower}} properties currently on sale in the same or similar neighbourhoods. Appropriate adjustments were also made in the sale prices to take account of the differences between the subject property and the Comparable in order to arrive at a reasonable value for the subject property.

{{/if}} {{#if methods.has_income_approach}}

 

2. Income Capitalisation Approach

This approach involves the capitalisation of estimated Net Income from the property. This is arrived at by estimating the Potential Gross Income (PGI), which is the total annual income the property would produce if it were fully developed and rented and had no collection losses. From the Potential Gross Income, allowance was made for possible rate of vacancy and collection loss to arrive at Effective Gross Income. The operating expenses that would be incurred in operating the property are also estimated and subtracted from the Effective Gross Income. Appropriate discounting factor is applied to the series of net operating incomes to arrive at the discounted future incomes which we aggregated to arrive at the fair market value for the property.

{{/if}} {{#if methods.has_cost_approach}}

 

3. Depreciated Replacement Cost Approach

The Cost Approach estimates the capital value of the property by assessing the gross replacement cost of the buildings and other improvements based on current labour and building material prices and also building construction techniques. An accrued depreciation based on such factors as age, state of repair, functional and environmental obsolescence is then estimated and subtracted from the gross replacement cost of the subject property to obtain the Net Replacement Cost (depreciated cost).

The value of the land is then obtained by the sale comparison or the market comparison approach and added to arrive at the value of the property.

{{/if}} {{#if methods.has_residual_method}}

 

4. Residual Method (Development Approach)

The Residual Method is used primarily for development and redevelopment properties. It is based on the principle that the value of land or property is equal to the gross development value of the completed project less all costs associated with achieving that development.

The process involves estimating the Gross Development Value (GDV) of the completed development based on prevailing market values. From this, deductions are made for construction costs, professional fees, statutory charges, finance costs, developer's profit, and contingencies. The balance remaining represents the residual value of the land or property in its current state.

{{/if}} {{#if methods.has_profits_method}}

 

5. Profits Method

The Profits Method is applied to properties where value is closely linked to the trading potential of the business conducted on the premises rather than to rental evidence. This method assesses the maintainable gross income of the business based on historical accounts and market expectations.

From the gross income, working expenses are deducted to arrive at a divisible balance, which is then apportioned between the operator's share and the landlord's share. The landlord's share is capitalised to determine the value of the property interest.

{{/if}}
